summary: Fast-acting benzodiazepine used for acute anxiety, agitation, and short-term insomnia relief. Strong calming and sedating effects, with real dependence and withdrawal risk—especially with daily use.
description: Lorazepam (Ativan) can quickly take the edge off severe anxiety, panic-like surges, agitation, and sometimes insomnia—often within 20–60 minutes depending on the route. It can also cause heavy sedation, memory gaps, and impaired coordination. Dependence can develop with repeated use, and stopping suddenly after regular use can be dangerous. Never mix with alcohol or opioids—this combo can shut down breathing. Best used short-term or as-needed, with a plan to taper if it’s been used regularly.

primary.context: Used for short-term relief of anxiety symptoms or as a bridge while first-line treatments (SSRIs/SNRIs and therapy) take effect (often 4–6 weeks).

off_label.context: Sometimes used as-needed for panic spikes or severe anxiety surges. Not a long-term solution due to tolerance and dependence risk.
May help short-term insomnia when anxiety, agitation, or acute distress is driving sleeplessness. Not ideal as a nightly sleep med.
Commonly used as both a diagnostic “lorazepam challenge” and as first-line medication treatment for catatonia.
Used in alcohol withdrawal (especially when liver disease makes longer-acting benzodiazepines less desirable) and sometimes to control severe autonomic agitation in withdrawal states.

common_adverse_effects.notes: This can feel like calm, sleepiness, or being ‘out of it.’ It’s dose-related and much stronger when combined with other sedatives.
Lightheaded, off-balance, slower reflexes. This is one of the reasons falls and car accidents go up with benzos.
Walking feels clumsy, reaction time slows. Older adults are especially vulnerable to injuries.
Can show up as disorientation, fogginess, or agitation—more likely with higher doses, IV use, or medical illness.
Local irritation can happen with injections; the risk depends on technique and formulation.

serious_risks.risk: Respiratory depression, hypoventilation, apnea, respiratory failure—especially with opioids, alcohol, sleep apnea, COPD, or high doses
Severe withdrawal syndrome after abrupt stop: rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, autonomic instability, hallucinations, seizures, and rarely psychosis
Paradoxical reactions: agitation, hostility, rage, aggression, disinhibition (rare, but clinically important)
Anterograde amnesia and blackouts (more likely at higher doses and with IV use)
Hypotension, arrhythmias, and severe oversedation (more likely in medically fragile patients or ICU settings)
Propylene glycol toxicity with high-dose/prolonged IV use: high anion gap metabolic acidosis with elevated osmol gap, kidney injury, hypotension, arrhythmias, seizures, mental status changes

safety.black_box_warning: Concomitant use of benzodiazepines and opioids may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Reserve co-prescribing for patients where alternatives are inadequate. Use the lowest effective doses for the shortest duration and monitor closely for sedation and breathing problems.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to lorazepam, other benzodiazepines, or any component of the formulation
Parenteral (injection) formulations: hypersensitivity to polyethylene glycol, propylene glycol, or benzyl alcohol
Parenteral (injection) formulations: use in premature infants
Parenteral (injection) formulations: severe respiratory insufficiency (except during mechanical ventilation)
Myasthenia gravis (listed as a contraindication in some labeling outside the US)

precautions: Abuse, misuse, and addiction risk exists even with prescribed benzodiazepines, and risk rises with alcohol, opioids, or illicit substances
Physical dependence can develop with repeated use over days to weeks; withdrawal can be life-threatening if stopped abruptly after regular use
Driving, falls, and accidents: slowed reaction time, impaired coordination, and cognitive slowing are common
Depression/suicidality: avoid routine use in depression or suicidal risk except for acute/emergency situations
Respiratory disease (COPD, sleep apnea): higher risk of dangerous breathing suppression—dose reduce or avoid when possible
Parenteral (IV) lorazepam contains propylene glycol: high-dose or prolonged IV use can cause toxicity

interactions.interactant: Opioids (prescribed or illicit; oral or injected)
interactions.mechanism: Profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death.
interactions.action: Avoid when possible. If unavoidable, use lower doses, shortest duration, and close monitoring for slow/shallow breathing and oversedation.

interactions.mechanism: Dangerous CNS and respiratory suppression; amnesia; falls; overdose risk.
interactions.action: Absolute no. Mixing alcohol with lorazepam is one of the highest-risk combos.

interactions.interactant: Other sedatives (sleep meds, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, gabapentinoids, barbiturates)
interactions.mechanism: Additive sedation, impaired coordination, falls, respiratory suppression.
interactions.action: Use caution, minimize overlap, consider non-sedating alternatives when possible.

interactions.mechanism: More sedation, cognitive impairment, slower reaction time; can worsen disinhibition.
interactions.action: Avoid combining, especially if driving/fall risk is a concern.

interactions.mechanism: Can trigger acute withdrawal and seizures in people with benzodiazepine dependence.
interactions.action: Used only in medically supervised settings; not a casual “reversal” for routine outpatient benzo use.

interactions.interactant: Other medications containing propylene glycol (relevant mainly to IV settings)
interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of propylene glycol accumulation and toxicity with prolonged/high-dose IV exposure.
interactions.action: Monitor osmol gap and labs if high-dose or prolonged IV therapy is used.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Sedation and functioning: daytime sleepiness, slowed reaction time, impaired coordination; assess fall risk and driving safety
Respiratory status: especially with opioids, sleep apnea, COPD, obesity hypoventilation, or other respiratory compromise
Cognitive effects: memory issues, attention, confusion; watch closely in older adults and medically ill patients
Mood and suicidality: worsening depression, emotional blunting, disinhibition, suicidal thoughts (especially in those with baseline depression)
Misuse risk: early refills, dose escalation, mixing with alcohol/illicit substances, multiple prescribers, continued use despite harm
Withdrawal/rebound: if doses are missed or reduced; monitor for anxiety spikes, tremor, insomnia, autonomic symptoms
Vitals when using parenteral routes: blood pressure, heart rate, and level of consciousness
Long-term therapy labs (when applicable): CBC, liver function tests, LDH
High-dose/prolonged IV use: monitor for propylene glycol toxicity (osmol gap, creatinine/BUN, lactate, metabolic acidosis signs)

special_populations.pregnancy: Lorazepam crosses the placenta. Benzodiazepine exposure in pregnancy can be associated with neonatal sedation (hypotonia, lethargy, respiratory depression) and/or neonatal withdrawal (irritability, tremor, feeding difficulties), especially with late-pregnancy exposure. Data on teratogenic risk are mixed and not definitive. When treating perinatal anxiety, benzodiazepines are generally avoided or used sparingly as a short-term bridge until preferred therapy is effective. Benzodiazepines are among the preferred options for treating alcohol withdrawal during pregnancy (inpatient monitoring recommended). Lorazepam may be used in postpartum psychosis treatment plans as clinically indicated.
special_populations.lactation: Lorazepam is present in breast milk. Available data suggest relatively low relative infant dose in many cases, and reports of serious infant adverse effects are uncommon, but monitoring matters: watch for sedation, lethargy, poor feeding, or inadequate weight gain. Use the lowest effective dose, avoid poly-sedative combinations, and reassess ongoing need frequently.
special_populations.geriatric: Older adults have increased sensitivity: higher risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle accidents. In general, avoid routine benzodiazepine use in adults ≥65. If used, start at the low end of the range and reassess frequently; initial immediate-release dosing is often kept ≤2 mg/day total, with careful titration and a plan to taper.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Oral: no dosage adjustment typically needed. Parenteral: acute doses usually do not require adjustment, but repeated IV dosing warrants caution because propylene glycol can accumulate; monitor for toxicity with prolonged/high-dose IV use.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Lorazepam metabolism is generally not dramatically altered in cirrhosis, but the half-life can be prolonged due to reduced protein binding and increased volume of distribution—so accumulation is a real risk. Extended-release formulation should not be used in hepatic impairment. In moderate to severe liver disease, consider dose reduction (often at least 50% of usual) and/or longer intervals, and use caution in hepatic encephalopathy.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral: readily absorbed; IM: delayed compared with IV
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Immediate release oral: ~2 hours; extended release: ~14 hours (range: 7–24 hours)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Immediate release: ~12 hours; IV: ~14 hours; IM: ~13–18 hours; extended release: ~20 hours

dosing.titration: Lorazepam dosing depends on the psychiatric use case—acute anxiety spikes and agitation are treated differently than chronic anxiety disorders or performance anxiety. The goal is the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, especially in anyone with opioid exposure, respiratory disease, older age, or substance use risk.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If lorazepam has been used regularly—especially daily—your nervous system can adapt to it. Stopping suddenly can trigger withdrawal that ranges from miserable to medically dangerous. The safer move is a gradual taper tailored to dose, duration, and your risk factors.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Lorazepam (Ativan) is a fast-on, calming benzodiazepine used when anxiety or agitation is spiking and you need relief now—not in 6 weeks. It’s commonly used short-term or as-needed because regular daily use can lead to tolerance and physical dependence.
items: {link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Anxiety disorders}: Short-term relief of severe anxiety symptoms
Acute anxiety or agitation: When someone is extremely distressed, restless, or escalated and needs rapid calming
Procedural anxiety/premedication (injection): To reduce anxiety and produce sedation or amnesia around a procedure
Bridge therapy: Temporary symptom control while first-line treatment (SSRIs/SNRIs and therapy) ramps up
off_label: Panic spikes or severe situational anxiety (performance or phobia-related)
Short-term insomnia when anxiety/agitation is the driver
Alcohol withdrawal (especially when liver disease is a concern)
Acute intoxication with severe agitation (e.g., stimulant intoxication) in emergency settings

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: It didn’t fix my life, but it stopped the spiral.
My body finally unclenched. The panic-energy faded.
It was like the volume knob on my anxiety got turned down.
I felt calmer… and also kinda sleepy and slow.
It was a ‘couch magnet’ feeling. Great for shutting off agitation, not great for productivity.
My brain felt quiet, but my body felt heavy.
items.note: Sedation can be the point (agitation/procedures), but it can also be the problem (driving, work, falls).

items.category: Memory gaps (especially higher doses or IV)
quotes: I remember before I took it… and then the next thing I remember is later.
I had pieces of the day missing.
I was functioning, but I couldn’t recall conversations afterward.
items.note: Anterograde amnesia (trouble forming new memories after the dose) is a known benzodiazepine effect.

quotes: When it wore off, my anxiety bounced back hard.
I started needing more to get the same calm.
I didn’t realize I was dependent until I tried to stop.
items.note: Repeated use over days to weeks can create physical dependence—especially at higher doses and longer duration.

quotes: Instead of calm, I got more wired and irritable.
I felt disinhibited—like my filter disappeared.
It made me restless and agitated, which was the opposite of what I wanted.
items.note: Paradoxical agitation/disinhibition is uncommon but more likely at extremes of age, with certain psychiatric conditions, alcohol use history, or higher doses.

sections.intro: Everyone’s nervous system has its own personality, but these are the patterns I hear over and over:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Lorazepam is built for speed. The exact timing depends on the route (oral vs IM vs IV) and the dose.
key_points: Oral: You may feel calming/sedation in ~20–30 minutes
IV: Sedation often shows up in ~15–20 minutes (dose-dependent), with very rapid antiseizure effects in emergency use
Extended-release peaks much later (often around ~14 hours) and is used only after you’re stable on evenly divided IR dosing
A single dose often feels like ~6–8 hours of noticeable effect for sedation/amnesia, but the system-level impact can linger longer—especially in older adults or with repeated dosing

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Lorazepam is effective for rapid symptom control—when the goal is to calm the nervous system quickly (acute anxiety, agitation, pre-procedure sedation, catatonia). The tradeoff is that the same properties that make it work fast also make it risky for regular daily use (tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, and cognitive side effects).
sections.clinical_details: Clinically, lorazepam is often chosen when rapid anxiolysis or sedation is needed and when a benzodiazepine that does not rely on CYP metabolism is desirable. It is commonly used short-term while longer-term treatments take effect, or intermittently as-needed for severe spikes.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Never combine with alcohol or opioids. This can cause respiratory depression, coma, and death.
sections.black_box: Concomitant use of benzodiazepines and opioids may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Reserve co-prescribing for patients where alternatives are inadequate. Use the lowest effective doses for the shortest duration and monitor closely for sedation and breathing problems.

Physical dependence can develop with repeated use over days to weeks; withdrawal can be life-threatening if stopped abruptly after regular use
Driving, falls, and accidents: slowed reaction time, impaired coordination, and cognitive slowing are common
Depression/suicidality: avoid routine use in depression or suicidal risk except for acute/emergency situations
Respiratory disease (COPD, sleep apnea): higher risk of dangerous breathing suppression—dose reduce or avoid when possible
Parenteral (IV) lorazepam contains propylene glycol: high-dose or prolonged IV use can cause toxicity
patient_counseling: No alcohol. Not “a little.” None. Alcohol + lorazepam is a dangerous synergy.
Avoid opioids if possible. If both are necessary, doses should be lower and you need close monitoring for oversedation and slow breathing.
If you’ve been taking it regularly, don’t stop suddenly. A taper is not optional—cold turkey can be medically dangerous.
Don’t drive, operate machinery, or do high-stakes tasks until you know exactly how it hits you.
If you have sleep apnea, COPD, or other breathing problems, tell your clinician—this med can suppress breathing.
Store it securely. Benzos are commonly diverted and misused.
If you feel paradoxically agitated, ragey, disinhibited, or ‘worse,’ report it—rare, but it happens.

sections.intro: Lorazepam’s biggest interaction problem isn’t enzyme metabolism—it’s additive sedation. Anything that slows the brain or breathing can stack on top of it.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If lorazepam has been used regularly—especially daily—your nervous system can adapt to it. Stopping suddenly can trigger withdrawal that ranges from miserable to medically dangerous. The safer move is a gradual taper tailored to dose, duration, and your risk factors.
key_points: Do not stop abruptly after regular use. Withdrawal can be life-threatening (including seizures).
Risk rises with higher daily dose, longer duration, and short/intermediate-acting benzodiazepines like lorazepam.
If used for weeks or longer, a taper is typically needed to reduce rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, autonomic symptoms, and severe withdrawal complications.
Lower/moderate dose with no benzo use disorder concerns: often taper total daily dose by ~20%–25% weekly as tolerated.
Extended or high-dose therapy, or concern for benzodiazepine use disorder: often taper by ~25% every 1–2 weeks, slowing down later in the taper as symptoms get harder.
For benzos with half-lives significantly under 24 hours (including lorazepam), some clinicians consider switching to an equivalent dose of a longer-acting benzodiazepine to smooth the taper.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Lorazepam dosing depends on the psychiatric use case—acute anxiety spikes and agitation are treated differently than chronic anxiety disorders or performance anxiety. The goal is the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, especially in anyone with opioid exposure, respiratory disease, older age, or substance use risk.

adult.anxiety_initial: 0.5 to 1 mg PO 2 to 3 times daily (immediate release); some experts start 0.5 to 1 mg once to twice daily in sensitive patients
adult.anxiety_titration: Increase gradually based on response and tolerability in 1 mg/day increments every 2 to 3 days
adult.anxiety_max: 6 mg/day PO in 2 to 4 divided doses (some patients may require up to 10 mg/day with specialist-level risk management)
adult.agitation_prn: 0.5 to 2 mg PO/IM/IV every 4 to 6 hours as needed (max 10 mg/day); in severely agitated inpatient settings, some experts use up to 4 mg per dose and may repeat IM/IV as often as every 10 to 30 minutes with close monitoring
adult.performance_anxiety: 0.5 to 2 mg PO once 30 to 60 minutes before the trigger; do a test dose on a different day first to confirm tolerability
adult.sleep_prn: 0.5 to 2 mg PO at bedtime as needed when anxiety/agitation is the main reason sleep is failing (short-term use only due to tolerance and dependence risk)
adult.xr_dosing: Loreev XR: Convert only after establishing a stable total daily dose on immediate-release lorazepam given in evenly divided TID dosing; switch to the same total daily dose once daily in the morning (for dose changes, switch back to IR for adjustments)
adult.catatonia_challenge: IV (preferred): 1 to 2 mg once; if no response in 5 to 10 minutes, repeat once. IM: 1 to 2 mg once; may give up to 2 additional doses at 3-hour intervals. PO/SL: 2 mg once; may give up to 2 additional doses at 3-hour intervals
adult.catatonia_treatment: Start 1 to 2 mg TID (IV often used first, then transition to PO as improved); may increase by 3 mg/day every 1 to 2 days to a usual total of 6 to 24 mg/day (higher reported in select cases with intensive monitoring)

sections.simple_explanation: Immediate-release lorazepam is the go-to for fast symptom control: anxiety spikes, agitation, and short-term distress. Extended-release (Loreev XR) is a conversion option only after someone is stable on evenly divided immediate-release dosing. The main rule is: use the smallest dose that works, avoid daily long-term use when possible, and always plan a taper if it’s been taken regularly.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Lorazepam can be used in specific high-stakes situations during pregnancy (like severe withdrawal or postpartum psychosis support), but routine long-term use is not the goal. Breastfeeding exposure appears relatively low in available data, but infants should be monitored for sedation and feeding issues. Older adults are at higher risk for confusion, delirium, falls, and fractures.

Lorazepam may be used in postpartum psychosis treatment plans as clinically indicated.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Lorazepam comes in oral forms for outpatient use and injectable forms for acute care. Some formulations contain excipients like propylene glycol or benzyl alcohol, which matter in specific populations.
items: Oral tablets: 0.5 mg, 1 mg, 2 mg (some scored)
Oral concentrate: 2 mg/mL (for measured dosing; can be mixed with liquid or soft food; sometimes used when swallowing is an issue)
Extended-release 24-hour capsules (Loreev XR): 1 mg, 1.5 mg, 2 mg, 3 mg (swallow whole or open and sprinkle on applesauce; do not chew)
Injection solution (IV/IM): 2 mg/mL and 4 mg/mL (contains propylene glycol; some contain benzyl alcohol)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Lorazepam boosts the effect of GABA, your brain’s main “calm down” signal. It binds to the GABA-A receptor complex and increases chloride channel opening, which makes neurons less excitable. Clinically, that translates to anxiolysis (less panic/anxiety), sedation, muscle relaxation, and anti-seizure effects—depending on dose and route.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Lorazepam is not the everyday first-line med for chronic anxiety. It’s a rapid-response tool: acute anxiety spikes, severe agitation, catatonia protocols, and short-term bridging while SSRIs/SNRIs and therapy start working. The clinical art is using it just enough to help—without accidentally creating dependence, cognitive impairment, or a dangerous interaction situation (especially opioids/alcohol/respiratory disease).

faqs.q: What is lorazepam (Ativan) used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: Lorazepam is used for rapid relief of severe anxiety, acute agitation, and intense distress when you need calming quickly. It’s also used in specific psychiatric emergencies (like catatonia protocols) and sometimes short-term for insomnia when anxiety is the main driver. It’s generally not the long-term, everyday treatment for chronic anxiety.

Oral lorazepam often starts working in about 20–30 minutes, with stronger effects building toward the peak over the next couple hours. IV lorazepam can work even faster, with sedation often showing up around 15–20 minutes (dose-dependent).

faqs.q: Can I take Ativan as needed (PRN)?
faqs.a: Yes—PRN use is common for acute anxiety spikes or agitation. The key is not sliding into daily use without a plan, because regular dosing increases the risk of tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal.

It can be. Lorazepam is a Schedule IV controlled substance and carries risk of misuse, addiction, and physical dependence—especially with higher doses, longer duration, or mixing with alcohol/other drugs. Even when taken as prescribed, dependence can develop with repeated use over days to weeks.

faqs.q: What happens if I stop Ativan suddenly?
faqs.a: If you’ve been taking it regularly, stopping suddenly can trigger withdrawal—sometimes severe and medically dangerous (including seizures). Typical symptoms include rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, racing heart, irritability, and in severe cases confusion, hallucinations, or seizures. A gradual taper is the safer approach.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on Ativan?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol plus lorazepam is a high-risk combination. It can cause profound sedation, memory blackouts, slowed or stopped breathing, coma, and death.

faqs.q: Why do benzos like lorazepam cause memory gaps?
faqs.a: Benzodiazepines can cause anterograde amnesia—meaning your brain has trouble forming new memories after the dose. This effect is more likely at higher doses and with IV administration. People may seem awake and functioning, but later have little or no memory of that time.

faqs.q: Is Ativan safe if I’m on opioids?
faqs.a: This is one of the most dangerous combinations in medicine. Benzodiazepines plus opioids can suppress breathing and lead to coma or death. If both are truly necessary, doses should be lower, duration should be short, and monitoring needs to be tight. Many times the safer plan is to avoid the combo entirely.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between Ativan and Loreev XR?
faqs.a: Ativan is immediate-release lorazepam that’s typically used for fast symptom relief and is often taken multiple times per day if scheduled. Loreev XR is an extended-release capsule designed for once-daily dosing, but it’s meant for people who are already stable on evenly divided immediate-release dosing (three times daily) before converting.

Sometimes, but usually short-term—and usually when anxiety or agitation is what’s keeping someone awake. It’s not a great long-term sleep medication because tolerance can develop and dependence/withdrawal can become the bigger problem than the insomnia.

faqs.q: Why is Ativan considered higher risk in older adults?
faqs.a: Older adults are more sensitive to benzodiazepines. They’re more likely to get confusion, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle accidents. That’s why most guidelines recommend avoiding routine benzo use in people 65 and older unless there’s a compelling reason—and even then, using the lowest dose with frequent reassessment.
